item.research_question: How can a hierarchical microstructure be induced in a single crystal high entropy superalloy (HESA) to achieve superior high-temperature tensile yield strength and ductility compared to advanced single crystal superalloys?
item.processing_route: Bridgman casting of single crystal bars; HT-1: single ramp from room temperature to 1,500 K in 20 h followed by air cooling; HT-2: HT-1 followed by additional heat treatment at 1,023 K for 20 h followed by water quenching
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests conducted at 298 K, 723 K, 923 K, 1,023 K, and 1,173 K with a constant strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹
key_findings: HESA in HT-2 state achieved a tensile yield strength of 1,023 MPa at 1,023 K, which is 110 MPa higher than CMSX-4.
The cost-specific yield strength of HESA is 8 times that of CMSX-4.
HESA exhibited a tensile elongation greater than 20% at 1,023 K, which is three times greater than that of CMSX-4.
The HT-2 microstructure contains a dispersion of nano-sized disordered FCC particles (4 nm radius, 4.3 vol%) inside ordered L12 precipitates.
The presence of nano HE-FCC particles contributed an estimated 110 MPa increase in yield strength compared to the HT-1 state.
The average L12 precipitate size increased from 143 nm in HT-1 to 153 nm in HT-2.
At 1,173 K, the HE-FCC particles disappeared, and the yield strength of HT-1 and HT-2 states became similar.
The raw material cost of HESA is 84% cheaper than CMSX-4 due to the absence of Re element content.
item.mechanism: The formation of nano-sized disordered FCC particles inside the ordered L12 precipitates is driven by the supersaturation of FCC phase formers within the L12 phase during the HT-1 cooling process; these particles act as obstacles that pin superdislocations, increasing the energy required for dislocation motion and thereby enhancing yield strength.
item.limitations: The metastable FCC particles inside the L12 phase are thermodynamically unstable and tend to dissolve into the surrounding FCC matrix after prolonged ageing (e.g., 200 h at 1,023 K) or at higher temperatures (1,173 K), leading to a loss of the hierarchical strengthening effect.
item.future_work: Future alloy design should utilize slow-diffusing species such as Mo to prolong the dissolution rate of FCC particles and improve the thermal stability of the hierarchical microstructure for creep resistance.
quotes: A hierarchical microstructure strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with superior cost specific yield strength from room temperature up to 1,023 K is presented.
The formation of FCC particles in HESA was driven by the supersaturation of FCC phase formers inside the L12 phase.
